chapter: Civil service, Keyhole club and civil rights
title: Post office special delivery job and the restroom incident
summary: Albert passed the exam and was taken for white; a supervisor told him to use the segregated restroom and he refused. He got a Black co-worker hired too.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: 1973, and we were talking about the post office and how the special delivery jobs were going to whites only.

That's right. And I had passed examination, so I got the job, and they assumed that they thought I was white. And I was driving a brand new Buick and some of these other old carcassers, and they had these old Model As and cars like that. The first real bad incident came up when I, after I was in there a while, I went upstairs and used the restroom. And the next day when I came in, the supervisor, I remember his name real well, was Ducco. He called me and says, hey Dominic, he said, did you use that restroom upstairs? Yes, I certainly did. He said, well don't you know that's not your restroom. Your restroom is around the corner, which was about a half a block down the street. I said, what do you mean? So he was trying to tell me that that restroom upstairs was for white only, and I had to go to the next one, which was designated as to. So I just, with the, I'm very hot-headed, and I just told him, I said, I may never use that restroom again. I said, but I want to let you know this, that if I feel like I need a restroom and I'm here, then you're going to have to get ready to tell me again about it, because I'm going to use it. Well, that didn't set so well with him, and then now they finally realize that I'm a Negro, and all these other white characters in there. And so they finally decided to open up another slot, there was a Negro boy there, his name was Conley, very nice looking fellow, he'd just come back from the Korean War, I think it was, I don't know exactly which one it was, but he had come back and they had given him a job. So this day I walked in there and I was sorting out my mail, and my car was parked in that little alley up there on Union Street, and this fellow coming in and renting and panning, and who was that old raggedy automobile for out there? So I told Mr. Duke Cross, and Mr. Duke Roller, after I sorted out my mail, he's talking about my car, I said it's not blocking anything, do you want me to remove it? So he said, yeah, it's going to remove it, and shut his mouth up. So when I turned around, I grabbed him in the neck, and it's going to hit him. So this guy says, cool it down, and he says, I'm starting up in the middle, so I caught myself. I knew I needed to work, I'd gone broke, see. And all of this is piling up within me also. So I went on the outside, and got to my car, and I used to carry a little piece of iron pipe in the inch behind, because the drivers around there were so irritated, man, I figured one day something might happen, and I'd have to defend myself. So he walked on the outside, man, there's a little cement porch, and I went and I talked to him, I said, look, let me tell you one thing, I said, I didn't come here begging for this job, I said, I passed an examination for this job. That's how he got it, and I said, boy, I know you can't even read and write your name, which he couldn't. But he had gotten a job in the days when you just could come into the post office and get a job. So he told me, I got to remember, well, what he was trying to tell me, I have to remember, this is the words of some of the old die hard crackers, as you call them. He was trying to tell me that I got to remember, he was a white man, and I was a nigger. So he never did get the words out, I didn't get my piece of iron, and I put it on his head, and I told him to finish what he started to say. Well, in the meantime, all these other carriers came out to see what was happening, heard the promotion, I told him, it's not me you're worried about, it's him, because I'd say if you finish this, tell me what he started to tell me, I said, you're going to have to pick him up. So they brought him inside, and Conley was standing on the outside, he told me about Conley, he called me after, it was a nickname that's going on. through the ages with me, he said, I was going to help him out, and we put out a switch plate, so I told him no, I said, don't do that Conley, I said, you're going to live here, I said, I'm not going to live here, I said, I can't live in this city. So I came home and I told Hazel to start packing, and we're going back to San Antonio, job or no job. So we packed up and we came back, and then I started working on Hayden, Fats Markins Band, which was the remnants of my band. But he was still a real contretto fellow, and he had his own ways, and he was, well I imagine, maybe I can put it this way, that the bar wasn't well, nobody knew, and he finally was getting to the place where he was getting sick all the time. And maybe that's why he was irritable all the time with me. So I stayed with him a while, and we played around him until I went to work in the civil service. And incidentally, Herbert Hall worked around me with us too.
Yeah, I got him a job, I got a fancy job. All the music wasn't doing so good. So I told him, I said, well let's go to work, let's give us a job.
